items.title: FF14 Devs Aren't Allowed To Talk To Lead Writer Natsuko Ishikawa At Work
items.summary: Square Enix veteran Koji Fox says lead writer Natsuko Ishikawa is snowed under and off-limits.
items.content:
By Greg Hill Published Sep 20, 2026, 10:15 PM EDT Greg works as a Contributor at DualShockers, mainly focusing on news content. He hails from the rainy Scottish countryside, but now earns his keep toiling away in the best city on Earth: Tokyo, Japan. With more than 10 years of journalism experience under his belt, he always strives to provide high-quality content that readers can trust. Sign in to your DualShockers account Add Us Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Developing content from one of the world’s largest and most popular MMOs is no small feat, as a new interview with Final Fantasy XIV devs has shown.

With so many story arcs, quests and dialogue scenes to write, Square Enix has started giving some strict instructions to their developers in order to keep work going smoothly—even if that isolates them or makes them lonely. And with the upcoming Evercold expansion’s branching narrative requiring thousands of dialogue lines, one staff member in particular is reportedly off-limits in the office due to their workload.

In a new interview with Anitrendz , long-time Square Enix veterans Koji Fox and Toshio Murouchi talked candidly about the pressures of working on such an expansive title like Final Fantasy XIV. They revealed that the scale of the work at hand is so massive that the team has been instructed to leave lead writer Natsuko Ishikawa alone, lest she get too distracted and miss deadlines.

Everything you'll need to hit the ground running when Final Fantasy 14: Evercold drops in January, 2027.

Image Via Square Enix Fox told the outlet about the rules around interacting with Ishikawa. He said: “We’ve been told not to talk to [Natsuko] Ishikawa-san, the leader, because she’s so busy. If we talk to her, then she’s not writing when she needs to be.”

However, communication with the rest of the team is more open, with Fox and the gang utilizing “Slack channels just for the localization and scenario teams” where they can “throw questions" and get answers immediately.

Fox went on to say that he still catches up with Ishikawa at break time, saying: “I talk to her at lunch, though. She’s always so happy! You get this sense that everyone’s so scared to talk to her, but when you do, she’s like, “Oh yeah, I’m so happy!” He thinks she might be lonely, but paradoxically, she wants to talk to everyone because no-one is allowed to talk to her.

Murouchi added that the team hopes to bring Ishikawa along to the next Fan Fest event, the most recent of which just happened in Berlin and featured scores of new reveals for Final Fantasy XIV . Fox said: “I think fans want to talk to Ishikawa-san more, but it’s so hard to pull her away! We need to give her a break and have her come over so she can talk with the fans. Everyone has so many questions, I bet.

Just give us the name of the second Job already!

The stringent no-contact rules in Square Enix offices show the massive undertaking that is the Evercold expansion, which will be the sixth full expansion for MMORPG Final Fantasy XIV. With new quests, branching stories and countless interactions to write and develop, strict deadlines and even crunch time will play a part in the expansion’s development.

Evercold will introduce a permanently frozen post-apocalyptic realm called the Fourth Reflection , strongly inspired by Norse mythology, and will be the setting for the next major story arc—The Godless Realms Saga. A new player hub, Fargarth, will act as the base of operations, and players can tackle the main scenario questline in any order they like.

Due to this player's freedom to explore openly and complete quests asynchronously, NPCs need to have programmed dialogue that doesn’t break immersion—each one needs a range of lines that accurately reflect the player’s progress and in-world events as they happen. That explains why Ishikawa’s workload is so heavy.

The Evercold expansion will also increase the level cap to 110, as well as introduce new jobs and raids. Players will be able to undertake the Basion role, wielding a shield-cannon hybrid and offering tank-like gameplay. One ranged DPS job is yet to be revealed , but will be available when the expansion launches fully in January 2027.

items.title: Digital Foundry offers a techincal review of Final Fantasy XIV on Switch 2
items.content:
0 It was a long time coming, but Square Enix finally released Final Fantasy XIV on Switch 2 this year. This is a popular and highly acclaimed MMO in the storied Final Fantasy franchise, now playable on Nintendo’s handheld console hybrid. Often with ports of big games like this one, the question is just how well they managed to get it running on the new hardware, and now we’ve got a video exploring that subject.

Digital Foundry has once again provided a technical review of a Switch 2 game, and this time it’s Final Fantasy XIV. This is a detailed analysis of the game’s framerate and image quality, as well as some special Switch 2 features. Their overall conclusion is that the game “absolutely can be a satisfying experience, but overall expectations should be kept modest.” See below for specific tidbits.

items.title: Final Fantasy 14 Is Bringing Back a Fan-Favorite Crossover for the First Time in Over Two Years
items.summary: Finally, another chance to get one of the best mounts in Square Enix's MMO
items.content:
By Willa Rowe Published Sep 18, 2026, 2:01 PM EDT Willa Rowe is a contributing writer at Polygon, covering games and entertainment. She is a New York-based journalist and critic whose work has been featured in Kotaku, Digital Trends, the A.V. Club, GamesRadar+, and more. She also co-hosts the Girl Mode podcast. News Finally, another chance to get one of the best mounts in Square Enix's MMO

Y'shtola is featured prominently in the Final Fantasy XIV: Shadowbringers trailer. Image: Square Enix Final Fantasy 14 Sign in to your Polygon.com account Add Us Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap It's official, Noctis is returning to Eorzea. Square Enix has officially announced that the Nocturne for Heroes event will once again be available in Final Fantasy 14 for a limited time. Players last experienced the Final Fantasy 15 crossover in 2024.

Warriors of Light can pick up the quest that begins the crossover starting on Sept. 24, 2026 at 1:00 a.m. PDT. You'll have just a few weeks to complete it and collect all of the collaboration's rewards, as the event concludes on Oct. 13, 2026 at 7:59 a.m. PDT. The Nocturne for Heroes event first ran in 2021 and returned in 2024, so don't expect that you'll be able to play it again anytime soon after this year's revival concludes. The quest line for the event sees the Warrior of Light aiding Noctis, the protagonist of Final Fantasy 15 .

Players can start the event by picking up the quest "The Man in Black" from Kipih Jakkya in Ul'dah near the Steps of Nald. If you've previously completed the quests, you can speak to the NPC to use the seasonal event replay feature. You won't be able to start the event unless you have a character that is level 50, and you've completed the main scenario quest, "The Ultimate Weapon."

It seems like somebody didn’t get the memo Square Enix via Polygon There will, of course, be plenty of limited-time items to collect during the event. The hottest item will be the Regalia Type-G mount , which continues to be one of the MMO's best mounts. It'll cost 200,000 MGP from the Ironworks Vendor. But that won't be the only reward to grab. Here's a full list of items and how to get them.

If this isn't your first time doing the event, you might try playing it on the Switch 2; It may unexpectedly be the best place to play the MMO .

Congrats on beating Dancing Mad (Ultimate), it was easier before patch 7.55

items.title: Inside Final Fantasy XIV’s Evercold Expansion with Koji Fox and Toshio Murouchi
items.summary: Fox and Murouchi discuss the Final Fantasy XIV team’s effort of localizing Norse lore, upcoming crossovers, and more in the Evercold expansion.
items.content:
Hopping off Final Fantasy XIV ’s last showing at Fan Fest 2026 in Berlin, localization director/supervisor Michael-Christopher Koji Fox and community and service division head and global community producer Toshio Murouchi headed to Otakon 2026 in DC to share the latest updates on the game. Anime Trending sat down with Fox and Murouchi to break down the team’s effort of localizing authentic Norse lore, implementing complex narrative choices, and anticipating fan expectations across major upcoming crossovers such as EVANGELION . The duo also reflected on the whirlwind tour, unable to hide their awe at the crowd’s fiery excitement in Berlin after the extended Evercold trailer, and opened up about the immense pressure and passion driving the development team. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Congratulations on the official release of the extended Evercold trailer during Berlin Fan Fest 2026! Fans are very excited that it’s coming out next year. Could you share your reactions and thoughts on what it was like in Berlin? What surprised you? Koji Fox: This is going to sound weird, but the first time we did Fan Fest back in 2014, we went to America first, then London second, and then Japan third. That was because the first time we did a Fan Fest, it was to get a first gauge of the fans’ reactions. Of course, we went to America, and there was the screaming, the moshing, and the crowd. Then we got to London, and they were [quieter]. They were excited, but they’re like, “I’m going to listen to everything the devs say! Please, tell us all the great things.” So, we had this idea that the European fans were going to be more subdued than the Americans. They’re both very passionate, but the way they show their passion is different. This time, we had it in Anaheim first. Of course it was [as expected], but for some reason, it felt like there was way more energy in Berlin. I have no idea why this time. People were pumped. Everyone was just coming up to you and hugging you, going, “Yeah, let’s go!” I think there’s this kind of excitement, maybe because with Evercold , we’re bringing a lot of changes to FFXIV . Naoki Yoshida-san (Yoshi-P) has talked about getting to a comfortable spot. When we released Dawntrail , there were things [we] were doing that were the same as [we’d] always been doing. Players were kind of asking, “But yeah… Maybe it’s time for something new?” and “What’s going to happen with the expansion?” Then, in Anaheim, we showed that first trailer and talked about how we’re going to change and evolve the game. I think that got people really excited because it was what they were expecting, and it’s also what they’d been asking for. You get the sense that the community thinks, “They’re listening to us! They’re going to start doing the things we’ve been asking and waiting for!” Now, there’s this real excitement that you haven’t seen for a long time, and it’s really pumping people up. I think that’s cool.

Toshio Murouchi: Compared to this year, Fan Fest 2014’s timing gap between the US and London Fan Fests was close to each other. Koji Fox: It was like two weeks! We went directly from one to the other. Toshio Murouchi: Now, we have about three months between events, so we prepared brand-new news and more information dedicated to the European event. That’s maybe why. Koji Fox: After going to all the Fan Fests, it felt like the fans were on fire at this year’s European Fan Fest in Berlin, which is really cool. There are a lot of expectations, and I think that puts pressure on us for these next six months to get the game ready and meet those expectations. It’s like, “Okay, we actually have to do this. Let’s go!” Evercold is very heavily focused on Norse mythology, from the name of the elaborate Realmships like Hringhorni to the everlasting cold era that preceded Norse mythology’s Ragnarok. How did the team work on the localization and research for Evercold ? Did you do anything in Europe that might have helped, for example? Koji Fox: The localization team is not just the English team; it’s the German team and the French team as well. Because we have those resources, they grew up closer in proximity to those areas. We have German translators who have that kind of knowledge, or they know other people with that type of knowledge. One of our translators knows a professor in Iceland who also knows Japanese, so we said, “Oh! We can go to these people to do research.” We did the same thing with Dawntrail . We contacted actual language professionals to get feedback on those types of Central and South American languages to make sure we were incorporating something that felt authentic and real and wasn’t just a parody. We’re doing the same thing with this as well. We’re really going through the paces, doing all of this research to make sure things are authentic.

When it comes to that though, you get really strange spellings, and everybody’s going to say, “I can’t read this.” We already have people saying, “Oh my God, I’m not going to be able to read all of that.” Unlike the Roegadyn language, which I made up based off of something that is mushed together, [the language in Evercold] is very real and difficult and based on Norse mythology. There are so many different renditions and spellings. How are you going to represent the thorn (Þ) letter? Are you going to make it a “d,” or are you going to make it a “th”? But we’re making sure we’re getting pronunciations right, doing the research, and then taking those into voice recording to try to make it as authentic as possible. Then, the localization team works with the Japanese scenario team and the lore team to make sure that gets across in the katakana, so everything is as close as it can be. They know what they want to do, so there’s a lot of work back there. I imagine the community team is just going to have to deal with “How do you pronounce this?” questions or comments such as, “I think this should be pronounced like this!” or “Can you tell the localization team that?” Toshio Murouchi: When we introduced the current expansion, Dawntrail, we had problems with new, difficult terminology like the tribal names or location names like Urqopacha. At that time, I felt for the lore team because you have to read it. Now, knowing about Evercold’s new lore, [Dawntrail] feels like nothing. It’s much harder. Koji Fox: That’s the decision the team made, and they wanted to do this. It was really hard to say Hringhorni on stage without thinking, “There are going to be memes!” It’s authentic, but there are going to be memes!

Since we just came out of Berlin Fan Fest, we saw some updates to the new MSQ mechanism: a different progression where we explore Area A, but you proceed to different routes, eventually connecting and making that unique experience. It’s kind of what you see in an open world, but with Final Fantasy XIV , we still have that main story. With Evercold , you have localization challenges and player experience to balance. Is there anything you’ve worked on in terms of mechanisms that help the player experience since you have to have different ways but still make it cohesive without breaking that immersion? Koji Fox: The biggest thing that’s going to happen is that you’re going to switch macros in the text that basically look at what parts you’ve already completed, and then character feedback is going to be different based on whether you’ve done Area B, Area C, or Area D. So, you’ll go to Area B, and a player will be talking to an NPC. Depending on whether you’ve already seen Area C or Area D, or if you’ve seen none of them and Area B is your first one, you’re going to get a different response about something, because your character will know or not know certain information. There’s going to be a lot of those splits, which means that instead of just one script, now you have four. It’s more work, but they’re making sure to do that because that makes it feel real. Because if you just have a split where everything is the same and isolated, then it doesn’t feel like your decision to do Area B first made any difference. People are just going to think, “Oh, it’s just a gimmick.” [The team] has to make it feel like it’s actually something. I think there are many things the team is doing, and those splits in the dialogue are one of them to give it a more authentic experience. So, when you go to Area B after you’ve already been to Area D, the [NPC] starts talking about things that happened in Area D. Then you think, “Oh my god, this guy actually knows what’s going on here!” and it feels more real. Since you’re going to have all these different switches and dialogues, have there been any difficulties when localizing this new style of narration across the languages? Koji Fox: We just started on a lot of the text. Some have come in, but a lot of it came in very recently. A lot of times you run into questions because there are so many splits [in the scripts]. Japanese can be a very vague language; sometimes it heavily takes on context that maybe isn’t there in the text, but is there in intent. It’s about making sure we communicate with the dev team and saying, “Oh, you are talking about this, right?” to make sure we get it right in our localization. That’s just another layer of communicating and making sure everyone’s on the same page so that we’re not accidentally revealing too much information. There might be a reason the Japanese is keeping something vague here and doesn’t want us to mention it. Or maybe because Japanese grammar doesn’t require it, we need to put it into English. But if we assume incorrectly and add something that’s supposed to be hidden, then that becomes a problem. So it’s this constant back and forth with the development team saying, “Okay, how much information do we really want revealed here? How much should this person know about what happened in Area D and Area B?” That’s why we have the localization team with the dev team at Square Enix. We have Slack channels just for the localization and scenario teams — we can throw questions up there, and they can answer immediately. We’ve been told not to talk to [Natsuko] Ishikawa -san, the leader, because she’s so busy. If we talk to her, then she’s not writing when she needs to be. But all the other scenario team members are open, so we have that direct communication and dialogue. I talk to her at lunch, though. She’s always so happy! You get this sense that everyone’s so scared to talk to her, but when you do, she’s like, “Oh yeah, I’m so happy!” Maybe she’s just kind of lonely because everyone’s not allowed to talk to her, but she really wants to talk to everyone? I don’t know! I hope we can see her at the next Fan Fest! Koji Fox: I hope so! I think fans want to talk to Ishikawa-san more, but it’s so hard to pull her away! We need to give her a break and have her come over so she can talk with the fans. Everyone has so many questions, I bet.

We saw a lot of new game design changes like “World Raids,” a tier between Normal and Savage, and even the Golden Saucer that’s coming up. What do you think players are most excited for? Koji Fox: I think players are most excited for butt sliders [laughs]. I don’t know when that’s happening, but over many, many years, it’s always been a definitive no, no, and no! Finally, up on stage, you could see [Yoshi-P] finally break — so now I think it’s not a question of if, but when. Who knows? Seriously though, I think people are excited about a lot of things. People who are really into battle are really excited about the new modes, especially because with every single expansion you add new actions, you add new stuff, and the controls get very complex. People get used to them, but new players coming in are just so overwhelmed with the three palettes, asking, “Where are my macros? I don’t know where to go.” This new condensed system, instead of three pages, is going to be in one. Everything’s going to be consolidated and streamlined. Somehow, streamlining it will enhance the feel of it, making a Dragoon feel more like a Dragoon. I mean, you saw the videos when they were up there playing [on stage]. I was just watching them while translating and thinking, “This is so freaking cool! How did they do this? That’s amazing!” Mr. Prime ( FFXIV battle system designer Hikaru Tamaki ) has done an excellent job, so people who are really into battle are super excited about that. We only saw three jobs. Now, you have twenty other jobs, and [everyone’s asking,] “What about my job? I want to see my job!” So we’re going to have a PLL (Letter from the Producer) later where we basically go over every single one of the remaining jobs. Toshio Murouchi: I’m scared how long that will be! Koji Fox: I’m so scared to interpret too! Oh my God, that’s going to be so long… It’s just going to be nothing but Yoshi-P going off, and he has so much energy. I don’t know how we’re going to do it! I’ve seen a lot of responses to that. People are just so excited right now because there are still question marks. We’ve told them what it is, we’ve shown them a little bit, but there’s still a lot of “Is my job going to work as well?” because there are just so many adjustments going on. What do you think, Murouchi-san? Toshio Murouchi: To me, aside from the butt sliders, the wide range of character customization will be a huge thing, because not only can you turn face paint/markings on or off, but you can also customize how you teleport. Koji Fox: Oh yeah, the action skins! Toshio Murouchi: Like Koji said, we understand how much you love your characters. Koji Fox: Every single fan you talk to gives you a sticker of their Warrior of Light. They love their Warrior of Light, and they want to customize it and make it more like themselves. Removing some of the restrictions allows that. Toshio Murouchi: That’s going to be huge.

In addition to these exciting updates, we also have upcoming collaborations, including Final Fantasy VII as well as all these other activities, including EVANGELION . With that in mind, you have a lot of different communities coming together, both from the Final Fantasy XIV side and from the anime series side. How has that been balancing the localization and the community-run side? Koji Fox: We haven’t officially started the EVANGELION stuff yet. They’re still in the design phase, and we haven’t received any text yet. I assume it’s going to be a challenge because it’s a crossover between two completely different series in the way that both approach their localization and their communities. You want to have respect for both. In FFXIV , we do have localization; that’s just kind of how it’s been. If we tried to take EVANGELION text and do that, I think that might alienate some of the hardcore EVANGELION fans. We need to understand that we’re bringing two together and find a happy compromise that keeps everybody happy. For localization, that’s going to be our biggest challenge — not just forcing the FFXIV way onto EVANGELION , but respecting what EVANGELION fans and their community expect. We have to make sure they have a similar experience in FFXIV and that they’re not saying, “Oh, this doesn’t feel like EVANGELION .” That would be the worst thing. We have all of these guest creators, and [Mahiro] Maeda-san is helping us. We need to preserve that. It’s such a storied franchise. Also, Yoshida-san is such a huge EVANGELION fan, so if we do anything wrong, he’s going to come down on us. I’m so afraid. Toshio Murouchi: That’s true! He’ll say, “Hey, hey Koji!” Koji Fox: “Hey, Koji! Why did you do this?” On the localization team, on all language teams, we already have hardcore EVANGELION fans and [assigned them] to work on this because they already have the love for it. We’re making sure someone who knows the series and cares about it is going to be doing those localizations. So, I’m crossing my fingers. I think it’s going to be awesome. I mean, just the music… [loving sigh]. Toshio Murouchi: Yeah… There was a tease of the housing system, inspired by other games such as World of Warcraft . Murouchi-san, you did your segment about exploring the different houses and different plots — what do you think communities would be excited for? Toshio Murouchi: At this point I can’t say other than what’s coming, but it’s a really good thing! The FFXIV housing system is already so nice, and as Yoshida-san mentioned during the press conference in Berlin, the team at Blizzard referred to FFXIV ‘s housing. They said they made their housing system better than ours, very luxurious and very nice. Now, it’s our turn. We’re referencing World of Warcraft ‘s housing system, learning from it, and bringing in a lot of elements, or maybe going beyond that. Koji Fox: We have to do that so that they will go, “Oh, no. No, no, no Square Enix!” Toshio Murouchi: Let’s see how it goes! But I think people can expect much more than that. From the community standpoint, I feel a lot of pressure, because any single bit people find out, they think, “Oh, WoW can do that? Why can’t we do that?” That’s scary, but I’m really looking forward to it.

FFXIV has grown a lot in the past few years with many new and returning fans. With that, you have different challenges in communicating with the community. Of course, you have a lot of live letters and live streams, but nowadays, X/Twitter is maybe more one region, and you have English communities on Discord and whatnot. What does the Community & Service Divisions team have to do to get that player feedback as well as the community input? Toshio Murouchi: The good thing about us is we have a dedicated team in each region. We have an office in Los Angeles and one based in London. So not only in Japan, but each region has its own community team checking their own trends in their specific regions. For example, in North America or the Western regions, they’re checking more on Discord or Reddit, which doesn’t really happen in Japan. Japan’s communities are much more X/Twitter-focused. Twitter is still a very strong platform. That has helped us a lot, so we are not focused on a single platform. We are trying to check as many platforms as possible, as far as players are on them. With the community changing how it’s doing activities, a lot of English fans used to be on X/Twitter, but now they have shifted to different things like Bluesky and so forth. Are there any tools Warriors of Light should be aware of that they can use to give their feedback to the Final Fantasy XIV team? Toshio Murouchi: Similar to the character customization discussions, we were more [focused on saying], “Be sure to stick to the official forums.” Same for global. We tried to make things equal for global and stick with the forums or X/Twitter, but now we’re changing to accept more options. If players want to use Bluesky instead of X, we’ll try to take opinions or maybe even open official accounts. Koji Fox: You probably saw the keynote back in Anaheim as well as Berlin, but it’s about giving players more freedom. Up until now, we dictated how you play and where you’d give us feedback. Now the shift, whether it be in-game and out-of-game where these communications exist, is about letting players have the freedom to do what they want. They don’t have to think, “Oh, I’m giving feedback. I want to use X, but I can’t use X. I have to go here, but I don’t have an account, so I have to open an account.” It shouldn’t be like that. It should be, “I put it here, and someone’s going to see that.” Toshio Murouchi: In the past we said, “Please come here to give us your feedback,” but now we’re going anywhere you are. That’s the major change.

During Fan Fest in Anaheim, that localization panel that you touched on in terms of Sinister as well as Dawntrail , are there any other memorable research you’d like to share that you had a chance to work on? Koji Fox: Oh my God! Seriously, that was not a lie — I was checking that out at work. I get from Kimura-san that we’re going BDSM, and I went, “Okay, let’s do this!” I went to Wikipedia thinking it was going to be wholesome text, nothing strange. As I’m scrolling, of course, some guy is walking by from the bathroom and goes, “Huh?!” I was like, “Oh my God! Oh my God!” But no, I love doing research. One of the things they consulted me on for Final Fantasy XVI was that there was an NPC out in a field watering their garden. They asked, “Back in medieval times, what were water jugs like? It can’t be like this. What kind of water jugs did they have?” So I had to go on this trip to find out what medieval water jugs looked like and where the holes were. They’re completely different, and they’re made of clay. I spent half a day on it and went, “Oh yes, I found this!” Of course, it’s used in the game, but no one ever sees it. But to think I spent half a day on that when I should have been translating other parts of the game! You go down those deep holes, and again, I love attention to detail. Toshio Murouchi: But I agree with you! It’s the tiny details. Koji Fox: It’s about making it authentic and making it feel real, but I love going down those rabbit holes. We’ll be talking about the water jugs, and that’ll lead to the type of seeds and the things they grew. You just go down the rabbit hole, and it never ends. Then half a day is gone, and you say, “Oh, I have to work late tonight because I spent half the day researching seeds!” With all these collaborations so far, anything you’d like to personally see FFXIV collaborate with in the future? Koji Fox: Wow… Oh, man! There are so many things I would love. We already did the Dr Pepper collab. I’m a super Dr Pepper fan — I still have the cans. I think that’s peak for me, so now that we’ve done that, there’s nothing else that could top the Dr Pepper collab! I wish we’d do it again. Toshio Murouchi: Recently we had a beer one, but that only happened in Japan. Koji Fox: We just did a collab with a craft beer place in Japan, and we got to do a tasting. Toshio Murouchi: Yeah, we actually designed the beer. Koji Fox: Yes, they asked us about the flavors and collected the colors. Now, you can go to a bar in Akihabara and get these beers. If we could do that in America, with some American breweries and expand it to cider, that would be great! Toshio Murouchi: That’s the dream. Koji Fox: And I’d get to test everything. I would personally do quality control for everything!

Special thanks to Square Enix for the interview opportunity. Stay updated on Evercold via the official player site or by following Final Fantasy XIV on Facebook , X , Instagram , Bluesky , YouTube , and Twitch . Interview article by Agnes Nguyen and Isabelle Lee. Interview conducted by Kwok Wai-Hanson.

items.title: Next Final Fantasy FFXIV Crossover Brings FFXV Back
items.summary: Noctis from FFXV will back in FFXIV for a time thanks to the return of a limited-time crossover event quest.
items.content:
FFXIV will get content from another Final Fantasy game again thanks to a rerun of the FFXV crossover. Square Enix announced that will kick off next week on September 24, 2026. This run of A Nocturne for Heroes is identical to the event that first debuted back in April 2019 , so there’s nothing new if you already met Noctis Lucis Caelum. However, this does mark the first time the event appeared since the launch of the Switch 2 release.

As usual, the requirements for the questline that begins with “ The Man in Black ” are a bit high compared to some of these crossovers or special events. You must get your character to level 50 and have finished the A Realm Reborn main scenario quest “The Ultimate Weapon.” If you have, then Kipih Jakkya will be at Ul’dah, Steps of Nald at X:8.5, Y:9.7. This starts a three-quest storyline that results in someone getting the Regalia Type-G mount and the Lucian Prince’s armor set that features boots, bottoms, a fingerless glove, and a jacket. Someone can also unlock Noctis’ Lucian Locks Modern Aesthetics hairstyle for finishing it.

Here’s the original trailer that goes over the event.

This marks the fourth time we’ve seen this FFXV crossover quest in FFXIV . Following the 2019 debut, it returned in 2021 and 2024 as well. This also means that this time every single platform the game is on will get a chance to go over it again.

Final Fantasy XIV is available for the Switch 2, PS4, PS5, Xbox Series X, and PC. Final Fantasy XV is on the PS4, Xbox One, and PC via the standard version and Switch, PS4, Xbox One, PC, and mobile devices via the Pocket Edition. The FFXIV FFXV crossover event returns between September 24, 2026 and October 13, 2026.

items.title: Final Fantasy XIV: Complete Edition for Nintendo Switch 2 Review
items.summary: FINAL FANTASY XIV Online Complete Edition is perfect for new players as it includes the base game and all expansions through Dawntrail.
items.content:
Final Fantasy XIV released on the Switch 2 as of a few weeks ago (depending on date of publication). I bought the Complete Edition , which gives access through Dawntrail … without knowing about the impending free trial version due out on August 4th. Still, I got 2 months+ worth of playtime to work with before having to get a Switch 2-specific subscription. So, how does it fare so far just after the A Realm Reborn expansion? Let’s find out!

Now, if you’re a Switch 2 newbie (like I am), then a lot of what is mentioned here will appear overwhelming to you, especially the plot of A Realm Reborn . Though, don’t worry, you do not need to play FFXIV 1.0 to understand FFXIV: A Realm Reborn ’s story, though having prior knowledge will help in understanding the context of certain flashbacks.You see, those masked individuals working with the Ixal (if your hometown is New Gridinia, more on that later) and in mysterious flashback cutscenes detailing the Primal Bahamut Dalahmud Moon that brought about the end of 1.0 are Ascions, aka: Paragons.

Their ability to summon creatures and possess people comes into play throughout A Realm Reborn and later expansions, and if you stick with it through all this story (there’s so much and constantly more coming into 2027 and beyond with Evercold ), you’ll discover the conflict between the Ascions and the Scions of the Seventh Dawn, with so many implications and events following these that I DARE not spoil. Yda and Papalymo are the first two story-significant characters you’ll meet, as a heads-up.

One of the downsides of Final Fantasy XIV: Complete Edition on Switch 2 is the need to pay a separate subscription fee entirely separate from the NOT-REQUIRED Switch Online. Yeah, in addition to needing any version of the game to play, nearly 150 GBs on space on your internal storage or MicroSD Express card, you also need a SEPARATE subscription to play the game past the free month grace period on Switch 2!! Yes, it’s annoying. Does it take away from the fun I am having right now? Hmm… a little. Thankfully, paying that fee is a bit easier than I thought. Just use the Nintendo eShop.

The game shines with its Xenoblade Chronicles -esque approach to combat. Each attack is on a cooldown after use. The more beneficial an attack or buff is, the longer it takes to recharge. Which attack you follow up with in combat after the previous one can offer benefits like increased damage to an enemy, for example, with the Lancer\Dragoon’s True Thrust following the use of a vorpal blade.

On the performance side of the gameplay, when dealing with less than 8 NPCs in one area at a time, like in a city or overworld, the FPS is generally 60, for BOTH docked and handheld (I don’t care about FPS as long as it’s stable and PLAYABLE). In the city or certain intense areas, the FPS is at a steady 30.

The music as always is excellent. the theme that capped off 1.0, known as “Answers”, is the most beautiful and best song in the entire franchise. Playing mainly in the raid dungeon known as The Unending Coil of Bahamut (Ultimate)’s final battle against Primal Bahamut, this song is masterclass in orchestral majestic bliss, and so on and so forth. I have listened to it about 50 times so far, with each time better than the last. It also plays at one other important point in the expansions that I, again, DARE not spoil, by the way.

And there’s so much more I even haven’t gotten into. Side quests, Raid Battles, FATE Battles, Team compositions for Raid dungeons, Parties, etc. AND, lastly, did I mention I’m STILL on the first expansion ( A Realm Reborn )?! I’m just now checking out the other two towns and their overworlds as part of the larger quest. AND I still have SIX more expansions after this to get through! There’s certainly a LOT of content here, which I can appreciate, but there might be TOO MUCH for me to do in such a short time.

If you’re looking for a Xenoblade -type MMORPG with memorable characters and plenty of engaging story beats to keep you interested, this game will scratch that itch, and then some.

My one complaint is the number of expansions and the amount of story/side content is a bit too overbearing and hand-holdy at times. Other than that, I enjoyed my time with FFXIV and the realm of Eorzea, and I can’t wait to come back for another adventure with the Evercold expansion in 2027.

If you liked this review, be sure to check out my review on Legacy of Kain: Ascendance . Thanks for reading, and I’ll see you next time.

items.title: New ‘Final Fantasy 14’ Job Leaked on Square Enix’s Official Site
Square Enix reminds Final Fantasy XIV players that the Switch 2’s free subscription period is ending soon
items.summary: Square Enix posted an update on its official Final Fantasy XIV page today to remind players that the free one-month grace period for its long-running MMO on
items.content:
Square Enix posted an update on its official Final Fantasy XIV page today to remind players that the free one-month grace period for its long-running MMO on Switch 2 will be ending soon. Starting September 7th, 2026, players will either need to buy the “Starter” or “Complete” editions of the game, or switch over to the free-trial that limits access to certain features. If you’ve already purchased FFXIV on Switch 2, your included month of game access will take effect on September 8, 2026.

This can be a little confusing to those not familiar with MMOs, but Square Enix launched FFXIV on Switch 2 with 30 free days as a means of testing the server stability on Nintendo’s console. Technically speaking, the game doesn’t actually release until September 7th, so Square Enix wants to remind players that they’ll soon need to start paying to keep playing. MMO fees go towards server maintenance and the development of additional content, of which Final Fantasy XIV has received six major expansion packs, so this isn’t anything new. This announcement is merely a warning so that people aren’t caught off guard if they suddenly lose access.

In order to pay for access on Nintendo Switch 2, players will need to utilize FFXIV coins, as Square Enix calls them. This is a separate subscription from the PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S versions, though having dual subscriptions will net you a 50% discount for access on the Switch 2 port. Basically, you purchase coins ahead of time and use those to pay off the monthly fee. FFXIV coins can be purchased from the game’s launcher, which will redirect to the eShop for completion of the purchase. It seems a little convoluted, but I suppose Square Enix is trying to conform to standards set by Nintendo’s online ecosystem.

If you don’t want to deal with any of that, Final Fantasy XIV does have a rather generous free trial. You’re limited in certain aspects, such as losing the ability to form parties with other players, but you can otherwise experience the entirety of XIV’s story and even play through the first four expansions. It’s certainly a hell of a lot of content for the low price of $0.

items.title: Review: Final Fantasy XIV on Nintendo Switch 2 is the best version of the game
items.content:
I have wanted to get back into Final Fantasy XIV for quite some time. I am a massive fan of everything it offers, from the art direction to the scope of the world and adventures that are held within it. I love the way that it handles narrative within the MMO format, and the massive range of locations to visit. I really, really love the music (I went to a FFXIV symphony and everything), and just generally the very Final Fantasy design of it.

Related reading: To think that I played this for the first time way back on the PlayStation 3. My thoughts back then.

But – and it’s a big but – Final Fantasy XIV is a MMO, and MMOs do demand a time commitment, both in terms of the raw hours you plug into it, and the frequency with which you need to play. Take a big break from an MMO, and it just becomes progressively more difficult to step back into.

I tried to get back into FFXIV once when I first picked up the ROG Xbox Ally . The device handled the game just lovely, but I’m not a frequent PC player, and so at some point I put the device down, took a long break, and just… let my subscription slip again.

I am, however, a frequent Nintendo Switch 2 player. By that I mean “daily”. And so now, with the game’s little icon sitting right there on my Switch 2 home screen, I’ve been logging in for at least a little playtime every day. I’ve already made significantly more progress than I did on the ROG.

Final Fantasy XIV plays just lovely on Switch 2, to start with that important point. The console’s screen is just large enough to be able to handle the very busy interface (it’s an MMO, it’s necessary) without distracting from the core action when you want to watch the fireworks. The game’s visual engine is just now ever-so-slightly showing its age with relatively primitive character models and textures – it has been going for something like 13 years at this point – but the art direction is still as stunning as ever, and I’ve loved revisiting my favourite parts of the world from my first playthrough.

Speaking of, I have started a totally fresh character and save file (I wouldn’t even be able to track down my original avatar from a decade ago, if she still exists on servers somewhere, even if I wanted to. I can’t remember my username, password, or the email address it was attached to). I love how it’s possible to play through all the base game and early expansions with NPCs, and not rely on parties of humans for the various dungeons. If you’ve ever played a FFXIV dungeon before, you’ll know that human allies tend to… well, race through it. One of the few unpleasant memories I have from my first playthrough of Final Fantasy XIV was getting to the very final dungeon of the base game and basically missing the whole thing (and being left behind) because I was trying to follow the story. The conclusion to literally dozens of hours of play.

Now, thanks to NPCs, you can enjoy most of the many expansions and all the stories within them at your own pace. And enjoy the typically excellent music, enemy layouts and dungeon design without feeling rushed, too. I even took time to take screenshots, which is one of my favourite ways to log my adventures in this game.

There is a downside, though. Because Square Enix wants to funnel players into the later expansions where, from their perspective, all the value to the players is, they’ve taken steps to streamline the earlier parts of the game, meaning that you accumulate experience points much (much) faster, and have to do far (far) fewer quests along the way. I have been exclusively undertaking the main quest line, with no side quests, let alone grinding, and my avatar is more than twice the minimum recommended level for any given quest or boss battle.

I understand why they did this, because otherwise it would be a truly intimidating, overwhelming task for a completely new player to get up to the newer expansions, but it means that those same players don’t get to spend enough time in parts of the world to really enjoy their contribution to the whole. The major cities are fine, but you’ll fly through little town areas where previously you’d spend a gaming session or two completing all the side quests. They’re barely blips and blink-and-you’ll-miss-them moments now, which really messes with the pacing for what was previously a truly wonderfully paced game that slowly walked you from one wonder to the next.

I don’t necessarily know what the solution is there, though if it were possible, I would have appreciated the option to toggle whether I wanted the accelerating levelling on or not.

Still, that’s my only gripe. The only other minor issue is that, when it comes to the chat, the Switch’s virtual keyboard doesn’t exactly allow for the same typing speed as a proper keyboard. I don’t even know if it’s possible to connect a Bluetooth keyboard to the Switch 2, as I haven’t tried yet, but even if it were possible, that would significantly undermine the portability of the experience. Currently I haven’t been social enough in FFXIV to require the chat function much, but I can see that becoming an issue later on in the game.

Those are only minor quibbles, obviously, set against a game that is hundreds upon hundreds of hours in scope, and now in an extremely portable and accessible format. FFXIV is a hobby all by itself, and now I can embrace and indulge it in full.

items.title: Final Fantasy XIV is perfect for the Switch 2
items.summary: Though it has its ups and downs
items.content:
Final Fantasy XIV coming to the Switch 2 is a dream come true for me; one of my favorite games now in a portable form factor. I’ve put a ton of time into the game on the system, testing just about every scenario I can think of outside of becoming a streamer and having a crowd of people follow me everywhere. Overall, I’m pretty happy with the port and can recommend it to players new and old, but I certainly wouldn’t abandon PC for this version.

The thing I and most others were curious about most was performance on Switch 2. I have bad news on that front, as you’re pretty much never going to get 60 frames per second on Switch 2 outside of certain cutscenes and exactly one area in one dungeon. It’s disappointing there’s no performance mode or anything, but you can cap your framerate to 30 in Docked Mode for more stability. Portable is also capped at 30, so you’re essentially getting parity with that aside from resolution. Your framerate can and will still dip below 30 in some situations, like running around a crowded Limsa Lominsa, but Limsa ‘tis a silly place. You can hear more about performance in this short:

As for visuals, the game looks good. Not amazing; there’s a lot of aliasing, and you can definitely tell the resolution is lower when going from 1440p or 4K on PC, but good. Resolution often screws with your custom HUD setup, which is something I was worried about here, but aside from needing to increase the chatbox font and move my job gauges a bit to the right, I was able to download my configs no problem. It moves seamlessly between portable and docked modes as well, something this version has over playing the PC version on Steam Deck.

Steam Deck might be able to hit higher framerates more consistently, but Switch 2 has it soundly beat in convenience and battery life, not to mention fan noise. I gave up playing the game on Steam Deck after Dawntrail launched, as just playing the game made my Deck scream in agony and it would go from full battery to almost dead very, very quickly. That’s at the lowest possible settings and with a lower resolution than Switch 2 offers. FFXIV will still drain the Switch 2 pretty quickly, but it’s far from the worst I’ve seen on the platform. Just make sure you don’t register for a duty at like 30% battery and you’re fine, or have your docked setup nearby.

Being able to go from portable to docked seamlessly here is fantastic, though the star of the show here really is portable mode. I love being able to do my dailies and slowly get every Job to cap while sitting on my couch, talking with my family, or just not sitting at my PC. Especially with the weather being so hot and my bedroom, where my computer lives, is basically an oven. I could even play outside on the porch if going outside wouldn’t melt me.

One of the best parts of portable mode is the touch screen. Sometimes navigating certain menus is just more convenient with a mouse-like setup, and just being able to touch the screen makes it super easy. In Docked mode, you can use either one of the Joy-Con 2 as a mouse, but I find this feature leaves a lot to be desired; both when you’re using it and even when you’re not. Playing with split Joy-Con 2, I found my fingers would often activate the mouse sensor, messing up my controls for a second or two. Playing with mouse mode… You just don’t have enough buttons to actually play the game unless you’re the kind of person who likes to click on their hotbar actions. You could plug in a Keyboard and just use one of the Joy-Con 2 as a mouse, which does allow for a left-handed mouse setup, but at that point you might as well just plug in an actual MMO mouse while you’re at it.

Another point of contention is that there’s no physical release. That’s not a big deal for Final Fantasy XIV as it hasn’t actually been on a disc in a long time, but on Switch 2 storage space is at a premium. Final Fantasy XIV will take up almost half of your console’s onboard storage at 108 GB. With Evercold on the Horizon, it’s only going to get bigger too. I actually bought a new microSD card specifically for this game, and am working on putting together a faux physical copy, complete with a game box and “cartridge” to store the SD card in. With… everything getting so expensive lately, I settled on a 256 GB card, so I’ll have to swap out the SD card to play my other Switch 2 games, which is inconvenient. You could simply keep FFXIV on your onboard storage and all other games on an SD card, which was recommended when the game launched as there were loading issues with the SD card, but I prefer to have at least some variety.

As of writing and most likely as of when you read this, Square Enix is offering all Switch 2 players a free month of the game. After that ends, you’ll need to pay an additional subscription fee to play on Switch 2 and other platforms like PC and PS5. If you just play on Switch 2, you simply pay the normal sub, but if, for example, you want to swap between PC and Switch 2 you’ll have to pay an additional half of the subscription each month. This is done through a weird currency obfuscation method Square Enix calls FFXIV Coins. You buy coins, then use them to pay for the sub.

First off, why the obfuscation? I’d really rather you just tell me up front what it costs without me having to translate and convert. There’s a reason Nintendo and Microsoft got rid of their points systems on their storefronts. Second, I know this is how Square got out of requiring players to need Nintendo Switch Online to play on Switch 2… but personally I already pay for NSO every year, and it’s overall cheaper than this weird Coin model; $50 a year for the Expansion Pak version as opposed to $70 a year by my math. That $70 doesn’t include an already existing subscription to FFXIV, by the way; that’s just on top of playing on Switch 2. I haven’t actually paid for my sub in a long time (thanks for literally paying my sub, Square!), but if I were to stop writing about FFXIV, I would be concerned about that additional cost. Being subscribed to NSO does get you an additional free teleport destination in-game… but I have teleport tickets; I don’t need that. It’s quite literally useless to me. In this situation, I’d probably just pick what I’m going to play on for that month: Switch 2 or PC.

Seeing as the Switch 2 version feels more like a nice supplement to me, I’d go with PC most of the time. In between MSQ patches, sure, I’ll take Switch 2, but if I go back to raiding or when there’s more story to play, I’d prefer the higher fidelity and framerate of my PC. I hope Square and Nintendo reconsider the choice of FFXIV Coin, because if they did, I’d shill this version as much as humanly possible. I mean, I’ll still do that for the game overall, but here I’d mostly recommend the free trial, then moving over to PC or being absolutely sure you want to play on Switch 2 forever. If FFXIV Coin wasn’t a thing, then you’d bet your sweet bippy I’d buy every expansion twice (read: once, thanks again Square!) so I could play on both platforms. For right now though, I’m pretty dang happy with this version.

How to Participate

Speak with the poor-heeled youth on the Steps of Nald (X:9.2 Y:9.1) in Ul'dah. Upon completion of the quest, you will receive a Yo-kai Watch and Yo-kai Medallium which you can use to obtain Yo-kai Medals. * Players must be level 15 and above to start the quest. * Players must have completed one of the following main scenario quests: "The Gridanian Envoy," "The Lominsan Envoy," or "The Ul’dahn Envoy." Don't miss out on this zany collaboration event!

Rewards

Visit the special site for more details.
